catalog_quote: Stress is not predictable, and so far its pattern is opaque. In contrast to an analysis for the Siroi language, geographically close to Sam but not closely related linguistically, stress in Sam is not based on grammatical class (Van Kleef: 1998); it seems that all classes can have either first syllable stress, or second syllable stress. In addition, phonemic stress does not seem to be involved ... Unlike Anjam, Sam does not appear to have minimal pairs differing only by stress. In any case, stress is not phonemic, and so is not represented in the orthography. Below are some multisyllabic words in various grammatical classes that have primary stress on the first syllable in the word that has an onset consonant. ... audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and both example lists are verbatim in the held / at pp. 43-44 as cited. (2) The deciding source is a 2005 SIL Organised Phonology Data sketch (10 pp) by the resident field team; it is short and explicitly provisional ('so far its pattern is opaque', 'more time.. will allow us to investigate stress further'), but Glottolog 5.1 lists no grammar, phonology article or instrumental study for Sam, and direct web checks (Glottolog Mindjim node -> Daniels ICHL 2022 talk; Daniels CV; Crossref) found nothing newer that describes Sam stress. So the record rests on the best and only available source, correctly read: unpredictable first- or second-syllable stress, non-contrastive, coded 'lexical' non-strict. sources.note: Only post-2005 linguistic work touching Sam; a trained phonologist's Minjim transcriptions could show whether the first-vs-second-syllable stress split the Troolins call 'opaque' has a conditioning factor (e.g. weight or a historical vowel) - the one thing that could move this record from lexical to a rule.
